No cardiac abnormalities were found on imaging. The Coumadin treatment is recommended for 3-6 months with target INR range 2-3, monitored closely by the physician.

The patient has acute on chronic renal failure with creatinine of 5.4 (baseline 3.5-4.0). Renal consultation determined the patient would require chronic hemodialysis. The patient tolerated hemodialysis well with stable blood pressure and no muscle cramping. Outpatient dialysis was arranged three times weekly (Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays). The patient will need to continue going to dialysis three times a week permanently.

The patient died from multiple complications including acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, gastrointestinal hemorrhage with ischemic colitis, and acute on chronic kidney injury. He received continuous veno-venous hemodialysis for volume overload due to left heart failure and steroid therapy. The GI bleed recurred after tracheostomy; he was found to be a poor operative candidate. Given grim prognosis, he was made comfort measures only and aggressive treatments including transfusions were discontinued.

The bleeding was caused by an upper gastrointestinal bleed from esophageal varices. The patient underwent emergent endoscopy with banding in the ICU. He was resuscitated with blood products including 4 packed red blood cells, 2 platelets, and 1 fresh frozen plasma. He was treated with IV proton pump inhibitor and octreotide drip for 48 hours, plus 5 days of IV ceftriaxone. The bleeding also caused hypotension and demand ischemia.

The patient developed ventricular tachycardia during hospitalization, which can be a life threatening heart rhythm. The patient was discharged home with a lifevest which is worn externally and will shock the patient if this dangerous rhythm occurs again. Additionally, the patient was started on Metoprolol succinate, a medication that will help lower heart rate and blood pressure by taking workload off the heart.

The patient awoke neurologically intact post-operatively but experienced postoperative confusion and agitation treated with Haldol and Zyprexa. He remained in the CVICU until his mental status improved. Psychiatry and social work were consulted to evaluate postoperative confusion with hallucinations. His mental status returned to baseline by postoperative day 9, when he was cleared for discharge to home with visiting nurse services.

The patient has anoxic brain injury after a PEA arrest during VT ablation, resulting in mild to moderate encephalopathy with stable reduction in gray-white differentiation on CT head. EEG showed no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures. He has a tracheostomy with ventilator support and PEG tube for feeding. The tongue laceration resulted from biting, requiring total teeth extraction. He is being treated for MRSA bacteremia and discharged to extended care facility.

The patient was initially treated with levofloxacin and Unasyn to cover aspiration and community-acquired pneumonia. Coverage was broadened to vancomycin/Zosyn on hospital day 3. After completing a week of antibiotics with persistent fevers and negative cultures, antibiotics were held. The patient has presumed pleural tuberculosis and is currently being treated with multi-drug therapy. Fever improved since induction of tuberculosis therapy.

The patient's intracerebral hemorrhage was treated conservatively with blood pressure control and monitoring. He was offered a Factor VII trial but refused, and there were no other alternative therapies indicated. He was monitored in the neuro ICU with blood pressure initially controlled using labetalol infusion for goal systolic blood pressure less than 140. Aspirin and heparin products were held given the hemorrhage. Repeat imaging showed the hemorrhage was stable.

The acute renal failure likely started from poor forward flow from initial cardiogenic failure and was probably exacerbated by 320 ccs of contrast received in the cardiac catheterization lab. She developed muddy brown casts on urine analysis. Due to hyperkalemia to 6.8 and anuria immediately post catheterization, she was treated with dialysis for volume overload and hyperkalemia. She is likely now dialysis-dependent.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy for necrotic uterus with abscess, then required second surgery for perforated diverticulitis with pelvic peritonitis requiring colon resection and colostomy placement. She developed polymicrobial sepsis with bacteremia requiring intensive care and antibiotics. At discharge, she was slowly improving with stable vital signs, decreasing white blood cell count, and required intravenous antibiotics and VAC dressing for wound healing. She needed rehabilitation for continued recovery.

The patient's pain was well controlled with Percocet (oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-325 mg). She was discharged on 1-2 tablets every 4-6 hours as needed for pain, to be taken with food. She was also prescribed acetaminophen 325 mg, two tablets every 4-6 hours as needed. The discharge instructions specified not to take Percocet with Ativan (lorazepam).

The bleeding gums were caused by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). The patient had several reasons for low platelets: end-stage liver disease, splenomegaly, critical illness, and multiple antibiotics that are reversibly myelosuppressive. The bleeding diathesis was related to platelet count rather than elevated INR. Aminocaproic acid was used for gum bleeding. There is no mention of oral cancer concerns in this medical record.
